Every value in these widgets is computed exactly, with rational arithmetic or from the checked format tables, and only
rounded for display. Where a widget is *about* binary64 arithmetic (the sums in the printing machine, the summation race,
the special-values table and the comparison playground), it uses your browser's own doubles on purpose: their +, −, ×
and ÷ are IEEE 754 operations, correctly rounded, so they give the same bits as any conforming machine (except a NaN's
sign and payload, which the standard leaves open). Each widget's
arithmetic is tested against independent references: Python, NumPy, the C library, and the post's own verification
scripts.

## The 8-bit universe {#universe}

Eight bits give 256 codes, few enough to see every one. Pick a format, flip bits, click a value, or type
a number to see where it lands.

- **Our toy 1·4·3** uses the IEEE 754 rules: an all-ones exponent means ∞ or NaN.
- **FP8 E4M3** gives up ∞, keeps a single NaN pattern per sign, and turns the top exponent into one more binade.
  That one rule change takes the largest value from 240 to 448.
- **FP8 E5M2** has the same layout as the top byte of an IEEE `binary16`.

::: {.column-page}
```{=html}
<div id="fp-universe"><noscript>This widget needs JavaScript.</noscript></div>
<script type="module" src="universe.js"></script>
```
:::

## Every format on one chart {#atlas}

From the 4-bit numbers inside AI chips to 256-bit giants. Right means more range, up means more precision.
Each extra exponent bit roughly doubles the range (counted in binades); each extra mantissa bit adds a bit of
precision. Click any format for its layout and limits.

::: {.column-page}
```{=html}
<div id="fp-atlas"><noscript>This widget needs JavaScript.</noscript></div>
<script type="module" src="atlas.js"></script>
```
:::

## The rounding lab {#rounding}

Every rounding rule makes the same choice: of the two values on either side of x, which one? Type a number (fractions
like `1/3` work), pick a format, and drag x between its neighbours to watch each rule pick. The table shows the exact
result, its bits and the error, both absolute and in ulps.

::: {.column-page}
```{=html}
<div id="fp-rounding"><noscript>This widget needs JavaScript.</noscript></div>
<script type="module" src="rounding.js"></script>
```
:::

## The adder {#adder}

How does hardware add two floats "as if with infinite precision" while holding only a few extra bits? Line up the
binary points, add, normalise, round. The trick is what it keeps of the bits that fall off the end: a **guard** bit,
a **round** bit and a **sticky** bit that remembers whether anything else was a 1. Pick fewer bits and watch it get
answers wrong. Use a small significand to see every bit.

::: {.column-page}
```{=html}
<div id="fp-adder"><noscript>This widget needs JavaScript.</noscript></div>
<script type="module" src="adder.js"></script>
```
:::

## The printing machine {#printing}

Why does `0.1 + 0.2` print as 0.30000000000000004, and `0.1` as plain 0.1? Every double owns an interval of real
numbers, the ones that round to it. A shortest-round-trip printer (JavaScript's, Python's) prints the shortest
decimal inside that interval (and if several are that short, the one nearest the double). Type a number, or a sum like `0.1 + 0.2` (spaces around the operator).

::: {.column-page}
```{=html}
<div id="fp-printing"><noscript>This widget needs JavaScript.</noscript></div>
<script type="module" src="printing.js"></script>
```
:::

## The summation race {#race}

The same numbers, added up five ways: a plain loop, NumPy's pairwise `np.sum`, Kahan's compensated sum, Neumaier's
variant (what Python 3.12's `sum()` uses for floats), and `math.fsum`, the exact sum rounded once. Each is measured against
the exact sum, computed with big integers.

::: {.column-page}
```{=html}
<div id="fp-race"><noscript>This widget needs JavaScript.</noscript></div>
<script type="module" src="race.js"></script>
```
:::

## The block-scaling lab {#blocks}

Four bits can be enough, if every small block gets its own scale. Here are the schemes from the post: plain FP8 with
one FP32 scale per tensor; OCP's MXFP8 and MXFP4, with a power-of-two scale per 32 values computed as the OCP MX
specification does, plus MXFP4 with that scale rounded up, as NVIDIA's MXFP8 training study recommends; and NVIDIA's
NVFP4, with an FP8 scale per 16 values plus one FP32 scale per tensor, as in its NVFP4 paper. Paste your own vector, or
plant an outlier and watch what it does to its block.

::: {.column-page}
```{=html}
<div id="fp-blocks"><noscript>This widget needs JavaScript.</noscript></div>
<script type="module" src="blocks.js"></script>
```
:::
